h: 4 Neither a public appearance nor tutelage
x: The idea in one sentence. The authors refuse to show themselves, because that would only serve a curiosity fed by science fiction, and to heal the Earth by force, because that would be immoral tutelage. The text, intended to be read at the Café Léon, imagines the scene of an appearance: autographs, torn clothes, the café renamed “space café”, postcards bearing the likeness of Fernando FSSesma Letter 1966 D47-1 p.206. It then asks whether the ideas would be worth more if stated “dressed in a fluorescent suit, in front of two hundred microphones” Letter 1966 D47-2 p.207. The harm, it adds, would fall on Earthlings, exposed to the “blind shock of hysterical masses faced with the sensational” Letter 1966 D47-2 p.207. On intervention, the letter is precise. A therapy “on a macro-social scale” would exist, but it would take “250 to 300 Earth years” to see its effects Letter 1966 D47-2 p.209. And it would presuppose: “a kind of paternalistic dictatorship, ruled by technocrats from another planet, who would treat you like children.” Letter 1966 D47-2 p.209 They judge it “immoral” to impose it by force. They add that they do not have “absolute certainty” that the Earth will end in a “nuclear hecatomb” Letter 1966 D47-2 p.209. They promise instead norms “that will help you individually” Letter 1966 D47-2 p.209. The fault they reproach readers with most is impatience: “TIME is necessary to assimilate concepts” Letter 1966 D47-2 p.209. No method fits into “some twenty typewritten pages” Letter 1966 D47-2 p.210. The same idea recurs in D47-4, which judges the expectation of a “SIMPLE AND EASY FORMULA” to be “DESTRUCTIVE and DANGEROUS” Letter 1966 D47-4 p.223 D47-4 p.224. This refusal to intervene will be taken up again in 1988 in the plan to save the Earth (D1378).

h: 5 A morality adjusted to each brain
x: The idea in one sentence. Ummo’s morality evolves with society, and each person’s obligations vary, within certain limits, according to the structure of their brain. The authors say they are forestalling an idea that “will surely scandalise some people” Letter 1966 D47-3 p.215. Their morality closely resembles that of Christianity, but it is “much more flexible”, for two reasons Letter 1966 D47-3 p.215: their theologians, the WOALAOLOO, consider that morality evolves with society; the “MORAL NORMS OF THE INDIVIDUAL are a function of their neurocerebral and physiological structure”. The child is assessed early, and is given the moral code suited to a brain similar to his own Letter 1966 D47-3 p.215. The consequence is stated plainly: “what is a transgression for one is not so for his brother” Letter 1966 D47-3 p.215. The letter at once dismisses the lax reading: this is neither “amorality” nor “moral freedom”. These norms are “rigid” and oblige everyone to respect the rights of others Letter 1966 D47-3 p.215. It sees in it, on the contrary, a remedy for the complexes that arise when society “hypocritically points the finger” at the person who cannot follow a common norm Letter 1966 D47-3 p.215. See also the chapter Justice, where machines assess everyone’s responsibility, and the chapter Spirituality.

h: 6 The shortcut that failed: remodelling the brain
x: The idea in one sentence. Ummo thought it could make a better man by rewriting the network of his brain; all the subjects collapsed, and society gave up this path. The letter recounts this episode over five pages, with a conclusion of principle. The techniqueThree-dimensional image of the cortex by the UULWAAGAA; mathematical model of an “improved” network; metal model of the cortex at a scale of 144/1 Letter 1966 D47-3 p.216. A double beam of gamma rays destroys a precise cell without opening the skull; other cells are transformed into neurons; a machine guided by the model carries out the plan Letter 1966 D47-3 p.216 D47-3 p.217. The experimentIn the year 5722 of the Second Time, ORIAAU 6 operates on “78 adult delinquents and 180 children” judged “mentally retarded” Letter 1966 D47-3 p.217. Apparent successThe subjects come out without memory, like newborns. Their re-education takes only about “15%” of the normal time Letter 1966 D47-3 p.218. A former convict becomes a recognised cosmophysicist, UROO 866 Letter 1966 D47-3 p.218. The collapseYears later, UROO 38 is found “like a robot”, incapable of willing. This is the ODAWAA. “Not a single one could escape” the same fate Letter 1966 D47-3 p.219. The explanationIn 1336 of the Third Time, GAAA 9 shows that the network of krypton atoms of the OEMBUUAW, which links the soul to the body, had disintegrated Letter 1966 D47-3 p.219. To explain it, the letter uses the image of a cone Letter 1966 D47-3 p.220. Man is born with his OEMBUUAW “perfectly balanced and stabilised”. The operation froze it in an “UNSTABLE” equilibrium, at the mercy of the slightest disturbance Letter 1966 D47-3 p.220. Three equilibria. h: 7 The long way: the IGIAAYUYISAA plan
x: The idea in one sentence. With no shortcut available, Ummo chose to re-educate the generations to come: from the year 5902, a new society was raised apart, on 30% of the continent. The scholars first list the causes of unhappiness, and the list repeats that of section 3 Letter 1966 D47-4 p.221: a brain structure often “insufficient and unbalanced” at birth, but reformable in early childhood; adults deprived of basic education, who infringe the rights of others; “aggressive reflexes” passed on to children. The letter insists on one point: this finding was made in a society “more advanced than yours in 1966”. Tyranny had ended after the death of W1WIE 1, in 1368.11 of the Second Time. Above all, “PRIVATE PROPERTY DID NOT EXIST AND HUNGER WAS UNKNOWN” Letter 1966 D47-4 p.221. Society was no happier for it. The social network was “too damaged to try to repair it in a single generation” Letter 1966 D47-4 p.222. The ancestors therefore gave up on seeing the fruits themselves. The letter compares their situation to that of a survivor who emerges from a cave after a nuclear war and sees his city in ruins Letter 1966 D47-4 p.222. The place“30% of the Continent” is set aside so that “the first seed of a society of the future” can develop Letter 1966 D47-4 p.222. The dateIn the year 5902 of the Second Time the IGIAAYUYISAA plan begins Letter 1966 D47-4 p.222. The methodChildren are raised from birth “OUTSIDE THE INFLUENCE AND CONTACTS OF THE PARENTS”, through an education based on the reform of reflexes. The link with the old society runs through cultural exchanges entrusted to “qualified persons” Letter 1966 D47-4 p.222. The justificationThe measure was “necessary at that time”, because the parents were not yet trained to raise their children themselves as they do today Letter 1966 D47-4 p.222. The account stops at the heading “STRUCTURE (AYUUBAA) (NETWORK) OF THE EDUCATIONAL PLAN” Letter 1966 D47-4 p.222. What follows describes the defects of Earth education rather than the plan itself. The result of the plan is not recounted in these letters. The timeline in the chapter History cites it from a later letter Letter 1987 D541 p.812.

The idea in one sentence. To those who see them as cogs in a social machine, the authors reply that Earthlings are more enslaved to their habits than they are to their computers. The letter itself formulates the objection. The reader might imagine them as “veritable mechanised monsters, without inner life”, coordinated by the XANMOO AYUBAA computers like the parts of an “Earth Clock” Letter 1966 D41-7 p.118. It answers in three stages. Earth freedom is illusory. Tobacco, advertising, television series, partisan press, taboos and prejudices would hold Earthlings in “a sclerotic and rigid mental frame” Letter 1966 D41-7 p.118 D41-7 p.119. Their morality comes from within. On Earth, respect for others would often come down to fear of the law, “a conduct imposed from OUTSIDE”. Among them, it comes from the awareness that it is madness to “make a leak in the ship on which we are travelling” Letter 1966 D41-7 p.119. Technology is only a tool. The machines are “simply AUXILIARY MEANS”. The Ummites also get used to doing without them, in contact with nature Letter 1966 D41-7 p.119. Finally the letter turns the image around. What would have “pained them most” on arriving on Earth: “You appear to us as puppets, moving with studied, convulsive, artificial gestures” Letter 1966 D41-7 p.120. The letter does not deny conditioned reflexes: it acknowledges that the Ummites have acquired some that direct their conduct, but calls them “rational and logical” Letter 1966 D41-7 p.119 D41-7 p.120.

h: 9 The game that sustains the network
x: The idea in one sentence. The OXUO KEAIA is not one sport among others: it is a single art of play for the whole planet, whose rules are calculated for each player and at every instant. The chapter Health presents the game as prevention. Here we find the criticism of Earth games, the history of the OXUO, its rules and its functions.

h: Why Earth games are not enough
x: A game with fixed rules cannot suit everyone or every moment. For the letter, it is not merely insufficient: “NOT ONLY IS IT INSUFFICIENT BUT PROBABLY HARMFUL” Letter 1966 D47-1 p.203. Chess engages only “an infinitesimal fraction of the neurons” Letter 1966 D47-1 p.204. Great players, moreover, would never have distinguished themselves in philosophy, theoretical physics or topology Letter 1966 D41-8 p.128. The letter also notes a paradox. Earthlings time their competitions to the microsecond, yet remain “so ANARCHIC” in the matters that count: social life, health, the economy Letter 1966 D41-8 p.127. It proposes reversing this scale of values Letter 1966 D41-8 p.127. It also rejects games of chance, lotteries and betting, which would aggravate injustice in the distribution of income Letter 1966 D41-8 p.127.

FormerlyPeople were advised to do 30 UIW a day of physical-mental exercises in the open air, between three teams, partly underwater, with solidified oxygen. Nearly 70% of the population adopted it Letter 1966 D47-1 p.205. TodayWhen the XANMOO computers could assess in an instant the state of a person’s whole nervous network, they could indicate to them the exact exercise to do. “That is how the present OXUO KEAIA was born” Letter 1966 D47-1 p.205.

h: Rules that no one knows in full
x: On Ummo there is only “one [variety of OXUO] for our entire OYAA”. But its rules are “distinct for each player” and “a function of time” Letter 1966 D41-7 p.125. They are so complex that they are programmed by the XANMOO AYUBAA, and that “the players never come to know the whole enormous complexity of the strategy” Letter 1966 D41-8 p.127 D41-8 p.128. The letter compares the player to the soldier, who knows his sector but not the general staff’s plan Letter 1966 D41-8 p.128.

According to D41-7, the OXUO serves to Letter 1966 D41-7 p.126: develop the whole body; stimulate perception and reasoning; “increase the gregarious and social tendencies of the individual”; form conditioned reflexes suited to age. Everyone takes up the habit from childhood, “without any pressure” from the family or the council, and keeps it “until death” Letter 1966 D41-7 p.126.

Several of these pieces of advice echo what Earthly philosophers and educators have written, sometimes centuries before the letters. The comparison is made by the author of the site; it supports the coherence of the ideas, not the origin of the letters. On UmmoRead in small blocks and talk about it straight away Letter 1967 D59-5 p.348Socrates, 5th century BC (in Plato’s dialogues)Maieutics: one advances by questions and answers, pausing on each idea before moving on to the next.Cognitive psychology, Roediger and Karpicke, 2006The “testing effect”: restating or explaining what one has just read fixes it far better than rereading it in one go.Analysis. Same idea, different justification. Socrates uses dialogue to bring a truth to birth; cognitive psychology measures a gain in memory. The letters, for their part, invoke “neurocortical reflexes” and above all a collective aim: creating “new channels of information” in the social network. Discussed reading thus becomes a social exercise as much as a learning one. The rule of blocks of half a page to two pages, quantified as early as 1967, is more precise than anything these authors propose.On UmmoNever mock, get those who stay silent to speak Letter 1967 D59-5 p.348 D59-5 p.349Carl Rogers, Freedom to Learn, 1969One truly learns only in a climate of acceptance, where one does not fear being judged.Paulo Freire, Pedagogy of the Oppressed, 1968Education works through dialogue between equals, not through the master “depositing” his knowledge in the pupil.Analysis. Here the convergence is strong, but the motive differs. Rogers and Freire defend the dignity and emancipation of the pupil. The letters add an almost self-interested argument: whoever humiliates others harms himself, because he impoverishes the group on which he depends. Montaigne and the letters join in opposing rote learning. The letters add a warning for adults: there is no quick formula, and asking for happiness in four pages is in itself a lack of lucidity.

A mixture that our pedagogies keep apart. On Earth, the two great families are often opposed: on one side the conditioning of behaviour, from Pavlov to behaviourism; on the other discovery by the pupil, from Rousseau to Montessori and Piaget. The letters combine the two: very thorough conditioning in the first age and in habits, then, for knowledge, teaching without dogma in which the pupil verifies everything. Discipline applies to reflexes, freedom to ideas. A collective purpose. Our thinkers aim mainly at the individual: his autonomy (Kant), his fulfilment (Rogers), his emancipation (Freire). The letters almost always bring education back to the social network: the adolescent becomes “a node of the network”, commented reading creates “channels of information”, mockery impoverishes the group. A technical precision. Where our authors give principles, the letters give settings: an age (13.68 years), a block length (half a page to two pages), a number of tutors (three), a priority rule (better to miss the end than the beginning). This precision makes their advice easy to apply, and that is no doubt why the “on Earth” part is the most usable in the chapter. A caution of their own. None of the thinkers cited tells his readers to be wary of him. The letters repeat it over 45 years, and add that their model must not be copied as it stands here. They present themselves less as a model to follow than as a comparison that helps one think. To keep in mind. The letters date from 1966 to 2012: these thinkers almost all precede them. One can see in this a convergence between two civilisations, or authors who knew the pedagogy of their time well. The chapter does not decide.

The idea in one sentence. The letters also describe practices that are disturbing; the chapter reports them without judging them. In the distant past, children were monitored and punished by electric shocks; the authors themselves say the result was disastrous. x: The idea in one sentence. Body and mind form a single network: mental state acts on the organs and on the immune defences Letter 1966 D41-7 p.124 Letter 1987 D791 p.857. The authors describe a “psychosomatic network” in which mind and organism react upon each other. Letter 1966 D41-7 p.124In 1987, two tendencies run through the person, entropic and negentropic, and act on the immune system: depression pulls towards entropy, and “the desire to live” becomes a health factor. Letter 1987 D791 p.857Man is a “physiological-mental unit”: serious disorders arise when body and mind do not develop together. Letter 1966 D41-7 p.118In 2003, they describe our collective state under the name “psychovirus”, a psychological pathology of the Earth. Late letter 2003 NR-14 p.1381 The same network in two states: when the “desire to live” prevails, signals circulate throughout the body; in depression, they slow down and die out. Illustration of D791.

h: 3 Play that heals: the OXUO KEAIA
x: The idea in one sentence. On Earth, play is used to treat mental disorders; on Ummo, it is used to prevent them from appearing Letter 1966 D41-7 p.118. OXUO KEAIA translates poorly as “play”: it is “the art of training the body and the mental faculties simultaneously”. It occupies almost all free time. Letter 1966 D41-7 p.117 D41-7 p.118Mental health rests on two factors: spiritual and religious balance, with submission to moral norms, and prevention through play. Letter 1966 D41-7 p.118Each game is adapted to the person and the moment: “a hospital does not give all its patients the same dose of insulin”. Letter 1966 D41-7 p.125 Letter 1966 D47-1 p.205They refuse to give “the recipe”: an Amazonian shaman entrusted with a modern medicine without knowing what goes with it would do more harm than good. Letter 1966 D41-7 p.125They criticise Earthly spectator sport, a “veritable drug” that buys an apparent social peace and perpetuates unjust structures. Letter 1966 D41-7 p.118 The same year seen twice. At the top, adapted play returns every day and tension stays below the threshold. At the bottom, nothing is done before the crisis; play therapy comes afterwards. Illustration of D41-7.

h: 4 Their diagnosis of our medicine: antibiotics
x: The idea in one sentence. In 1966, the letter “Preventive medicine on Earth” announces that our antibiotics are producing resistant microbes Letter 1966 D46 p.199. “In a future of 180 years, plus or minus 10%, 72% of the species catalogued by you will be as virulent as before the appearance of these medicines.” Letter 1966 D46 p.199They add that this should not alarm us too much: our biochemists will by then have taken “a gigantic step”. Letter 1966 D46 p.199Our therapeutics progresses mainly with general science (diathermy, laser for the retina, Markov chains for diagnosis); they give only simple advice. Letter 1966 D46 p.200In 1987, on the telephone, a speaker describes AIDS as a virus manufactured in a laboratory in Ohio and released by an escaped monkey, “something similar to what happened to us in Albacete”. The claim is reported as it stands. Conversation 1987 H4 p.1288 A diagram, not a measurement. ① 1945: in his Nobel lecture, Fleming warns that the overuse of penicillin will select for resistant microbes. ② 1966: letter D46. ③ 2019: 1.27 million deaths directly attributable to resistant bacteria (The Lancet, 2022). ④ Around 2146: the letter’s forecast, 72% of species.

The idea in one sentence. The body could live for more than 140 years, but the Ummites choose to die between 91 and 121 years, when the brain begins to lose telepathy and then memory Late letter 2003 NR-18 p.1393. This cerebral degeneration, they say, they can neither avoid nor wish to avoid; the loss of autonomy is “an unacceptable attack” on dignity. Late letter 2003 NR-18 p.1393On the telephone, in 1987: suicide is a mental illness; euthanasia is lawful under conditions, with the patient’s consent, when life is irreversibly impaired. Conversation 1987 H8 p.1303 The ceremony of chosen death is described in the animation “An Ummite life” in the chapter Meta-biology.

h: 6 The beginning of life: the letter on abortion
x: The idea in one sentence. The 1987 letter proposes a method rather than a verdict: the value of life grows with the complexity of the living network Letter 1987 D539 p.797 D539 p.799. Abortion is almost unknown on Ummo, thanks to control of the genome and to a gestation assisted by biotechnology, never in vitro. Letter 1987 D539 p.798Life is a negentropic network; an isolated organ is a network in the same way as a mammal or a conifer. Letter 1987 D539 p.799The network of krypton atoms forms from the moment of fertilisation. Letter 1987 D539 p.799 D539 p.802The debate over when the embryo becomes a “person” is judged sterile; moral gravity is graduated from the zygote to the embryo and then to the foetus. Letter 1987 D539 p.801 D539 p.803The violations of the moral law cited side by side: killing an embryo on a whim, the bullfight, famine, terrorism. Letter 1987 D539 p.804The 1966 letters also say that the rare cases of hypersexuality are isolated and treated, and that homosexuality is “controlled” hormonally. Letter 1966 D41-12 p.143 A continuous scale rather than a date: the living network grows more complex from the zygote to the foetus, and the gravity of ending it increases with it. Illustration of D539.

The idea in one sentence. They say they eradicated cancer by genetic mutation but refuse to pass the technique on to us Letter 1980 D118 p.684. The same technique could be used to create “self-resistant” microbes for biological warfare, or “virtually decerebrate” beings used as slaves. Letter 1980 D118 p.684In 1988, however, their “plan to save the Earth” offers diagrams for protein production and formulas against AIDS. Letter 1988 D1378 p.912

The idea in one sentence. It is the only account in which the authors say they are responsible for medical harm on Earth Letter 1971 D108 p.649 D108 p.651. An imported virus, harmless to healthy tissue, multiplied only in dying tissue; it affected Margarita Ruiz de Lihori, who was suffering from nephropathy and leukaemia. Letter 1971 D108 p.649 D108 p.650The area was sterilised, but a residual focus in a man’s lung could not be destroyed without his consent. Letter 1971 D108 p.651The vivisected animals were anaesthetised; the brothers presented themselves as “Danish doctors”. Letter 1987 D357-1 p.718

The comparison with thinkers and institutions of Earth is made by the author of the site; it sheds light on the ideas of the letters, and says nothing about their origin. On UmmoPrevent before curing Letter 1966 D41-7 p.117 D41-7 p.118Hippocrates, 5th century BCThe “regimen” of life (diet, exercise, sleep) as the first medicine.OMS, 1946Health is “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being”, not merely the absence of disease.Aaron Antonovsky, 1979Salutogenesis: looking for what keeps people healthy rather than what makes them ill.Analysis. The idea is the starting point of our own medicine. The difference is practical: our systems mostly fund treatment, and prevention receives only a small share of spending. The letters describe the opposite, made possible by two tools we do not have, mastery of the genome and an entirely planned society. The lesson that can be carried over is therefore budgetary and cultural more than technical.On UmmoBody and mind form a single network Letter 1966 D41-7 p.124 Letter 1987 D791 p.857Georg Groddeck and Franz Alexander, 1920-1950Psychosomatic medicine: some illnesses of the body have a psychic component.George Engel, 1977The biopsychosocial model: every illness has biological, psychological and social dimensions.Psychoneuroimmunology, since the 1980sChronic stress and depression measurably weaken immunity.Analysis. On this point, our science caught up with the letters after 1966: the link between mental state and immunity is now documented. Only the framework differs: the letters speak of entropy and negentropy, a notion they use everywhere (morality, economics, health), where we speak of stress hormones and inflammation.On UmmoPlay as prevention Letter 1966 D41-7 p.118Johan Huizinga, 1938Homo ludens: play is a function of culture, not a mere pastime.Donald Winnicott, 1971Playing and Reality: playing is the condition of psychic health; an adult who no longer plays is suffering.Juvenal, 2nd century“Bread and circuses”: the spectacle that keeps the people quiet, which the letters hold against spectator sport.Analysis. Winnicott is the closest: the letters turn his intuition into an institution, with an individual dosage as for a medicine. They also distinguish two kinds of play that we confuse: the kind one practises, which trains body and mind together, and the kind one watches, which lulls. This is the most applicable element of the chapter.On UmmoAntibiotic resistance Letter 1966 D46 p.199Alexander Fleming, 1945In his Nobel lecture, he announces that the poorly dosed use of penicillin will select for resistant microbes.O’Neill Report, 2016Up to 10 million deaths a year by 2050 if nothing changes.OMSAntimicrobial resistance ranks among the ten greatest threats to global health.Analysis. The 1966 warning was not unknown to specialists, but it was absent from public debate. What has changed is the pace: our figures describe a present problem, whereas the letter placed it over two centuries. The percentage and the timescale cannot be verified; the direction of the forecast is confirmed.On UmmoDying when one decides Late letter 2003 NR-18 p.1393 Conversation 1987 H8 p.1303Seneca, 1st centuryLetters to Lucilius: he accepts departing if the mind comes undone, rather than outliving oneself.Netherlands and Belgium 2002, Canada 2016Assisted-dying laws based on unbearable suffering and serious illness; France has been debating the issue in Parliament in recent years.Analysis. The letters’ criterion is precise: it is not suffering but the loss of the faculties that make the person (telepathy, memory). This is exactly Seneca’s position. Our laws almost all rest on suffering and incurable illness, and dementia alone remains the most disputed case there. The letters place the cursor where our legislation hesitates most.On UmmoThe beginning of life Letter 1987 D539 p.799 D539 p.801AristotleThe soul arrives in stages: life develops before becoming fully human.Veil Law, 1975Termination of pregnancy regulated by a legal time limit.National Consultative Ethics Committee, 1984The embryo is a “potential human person”.Analysis. The letters’ position is graduated, like our laws, but for a different reason: value grows with the complexity of the living network, and not with a date or a threshold of viability. It is a continuous scale where our laws set a time limit. It allows abortion “on a whim” to be condemned without making the embryo a person.

Few ideas unknown on Earth. Hippocrates, Winnicott, Engel or Seneca formulated the same intuitions. What distinguishes Ummo is that these ideas are applied there together and for everyone, with a tool, the genome, that we lack. Two verifiable predictions. Antibiotic resistance and the link between mind and immunity go in the direction of what science has established since 1966. An original criterion. On death as on the beginning of life, the letters reason neither in terms of suffering nor of dates, but of the complexity of the living network: this is their most singular contribution to the debate.

The idea in one sentence. The letters on health complement one another, but leave several questions open; the chapter reports them without deciding. Refusing, then offering: a refusal to pass on their techniques in 1966 and in 1980, then an offer of a health plan and formulas against AIDS in 1988. Letter 1966 D46 p.199 Letter 1980 D118 p.684 Letter 1988 D1378 p.912The degeneration they “do not want” to avoid: the text does not say why a medicine capable of compensating for everything else chooses not to treat the brain. Late letter 2003 NR-18 p.1393The AIDS from Ohio: the claim comes from a telephone conversation, not from a letter, and is supported by no verifiable evidence. II · Ummo according to the letters › Society›Chapter 16 of 31Society · Chapter 16Justice and punishment A justice that seeks to educate rather than punish, where machines make assessments and shame replaces prison. From one letter to the next, however, the doctrine changes, and that change is a thread of the chapter. 5 lettersthree doctrines of justice between 1966 and 1987 D33-3 p.49 D68-1 p.427 D791 p.8550death penalty, according to the 1966 letter D33-3 p.4960 uiw≈ 3 h a day of re-education for the convict D33-3 p.492damages: the visible one and the one done to the BB D791 p.855

The idea in one sentence. In 1967, the authors themselves compare their laws (UAA) with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and see in it a “very significant analogy” Letter 1967 D68-1 p.428. Their list echoes our rights: equality before the law, freedom of association, free parties and trade unions, the right to strike, inviolability of correspondence, the right not to be arbitrarily detained. Letter 1967 D68-1 p.428 D68-1 p.429They add rights of their own: access to all information, demanding from a superior the reasons for his conduct, and discussing his orders. Letter 1967 D68-1 p.429The law stands above the Council itself; the legislative, judicial and executive powers do not depend on the same body. Letter 1967 D68-1 p.427No one may be ignorant of the law: in case of doubt, everyone asks the XANMOO AYUBAA about their rights and obligations. Letter 1967 D68-1 p.426

The idea in one sentence. The letters give three answers: the machine (1966), humans assisted by the machine (1967), then machines again (1987). 1966: no court “as on Earth”. Criminal responsibility and the penalty are weighed according to a single legal code by the XANMOO network (120 computers). Letter 1966 D33-3 p.491967: the OMMOI DOOXOO, the judicial function of the UMMOAELEWEEANNI council, interprets transgressions and applies sanctions. It relies on the person’s testimony and on XANMOO data, but the machine does not judge. Letter 1967 D68-1 p.4271987: judge, jury and experts are intelligent machines; superiors then dictate the “educating reagent”. Letter 1987 D791 p.855

The idea in one sentence. The sanction is not vengeance: it must correct, and “we neither chastise nor sanction” Letter 1987 D791 p.855. In 1967, only a conscious transgression is sanctioned: “we have effective means” to distinguish the compulsive act from free will. The guilty person purifies himself by serving the community. Letter 1967 D68-1 p.424The laws are severe for offences against the social network; a fault against the collectivity weighs more than a fault against an isolated brother. Letter 1967 D68-1 p.424 Letter 1966 D41-9 p.131In 1987, the fault is followed by an aversion shock intended to educate; learning proceeds by trial, error and reward, as with the child. Letter 1987 D791 p.855 The “educating reagent” extends the chapter Education: justice is described there as an education continued into adulthood.

The idea in one sentence. The most frequently described punishment is stripping, a humiliation “very important for our psychology”, brief and without mockery Letter 1967 D57-3 p.270 Letter 1972 D102 p.607. The lightest penalty consists in appearing naked before one’s superior. Letter 1967 D57-3 p.270“No one will rejoice in their inner self, no one will take advantage of the accused’s terrible shame to amuse themselves”; everyone hopes that the penalty will be brief and that the brother can dress again. Letter 1972 D102 p.607The penalty also has an educational role: the condemned are used for practical anatomy work, and their small number is a problem for the teachers. Letter 1972 D102 p.607“In vivo” experiments are “radically prohibited” on humans as on evolved animals; only those that do not harm the body and cause no pain are tolerated. Letter 1972 D102 p.607Accumulated merits make it possible to cancel the nakedness. Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49 Two kinds of shame. At the pillory, the crowd mocks and the exclusion lasts. In the scene described by D102, the witnesses lower their eyes and hope that the penalty will be brief; one of them brings the tunic (in orange) and gives it back to the condemned man.

h: 5 The convict in the service of all
x: The idea in one sentence. In the 1966 letter, the offender becomes “property of the People”, who employ him in dangerous tasks or in experiments, without making him suffer or putting him in danger of death Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49. He is presented undressed to inhabitants who take symbolic possession of him; society uses him for biological experiments and for work at great depth or in dangerous conditions. Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49Every means is used to preserve his life and protect him from pain; deadly or mutilating experiments are forbidden. Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49There is no remission of sentence, but merits are rewarded, and 60 uiw a day (about 3 hours) are devoted to his spiritual and technical re-education. Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49The penal population is “very small”. The example that opens the passage is that of a 15-year-old girl who had killed her sister by electrocution, studied during the discovery of cerebral krypton. Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49

The idea in one sentence. In 1987, Ummite justice no longer judges intent: it measures the damage and corrects; the moral fault is “compensated” by the BB after death Letter 1987 D791 p.855 D791 p.856. The authors begin with: “we too violate moral laws”. Letter 1987 D791 p.854Two kinds of damage: UIWEEXII, the visible damage, and WOAAWUUYAA, that done to the BB and to the multicosmos. Letter 1987 D791 p.855The damage, the circumstances and the psychophysiological state of the person are assessed; our insistence on intent seems “aberrant” to them. Letter 1987 D791 p.855 D791 p.856Free will exists but it is narrow: the genome, the pressures of the hypothalamus and the krypton atoms leave a small margin. Letter 1987 D791 p.856A saying attributed to UUMMOWOA points the same way: why accuse one’s brother, if his act has its source in the laws that govern the body? Letter 1966 D43 p.186 Two ways of weighing the same act. The earthly judge weighs intent above all: without it, no crime. The 1987 machine measures only the damage and deduces the correction from it; the moral fault is left to the BB.

The idea in one sentence. Present-day justice is born of a trauma: two despotic reigns, then a collegial power that can never be exercised by a single person Letter 1966 D41-15 p.154 D41-15 p.156 Letter 1967 D68-2 p.431. I4IE 456 has nine of his twelve councillors executed and proclaims himself absolute leader in the name of scientific progress, relying on a philosophy that denies human freedom. Letter 1966 D41-15 p.154 D41-15 p.169His daughter W1WIE 1, who is not yet 14, requires all fertile women to be pregnant; the police strip in public those who feign it; at least four million victims are counted. Letter 1966 D41-12 p.142 Letter 1966 D41-15 p.156After his death, power becomes collegial: the UMMOAELEWEE, four members at most, never one alone. Letter 1966 D41-15 p.156 Letter 1967 D68-2 p.431Nakedness, a tool of terror under W1WIE 1, later becomes the ordinary penalty, but regulated and without mockery. Letter 1966 D41-12 p.142 Letter 1972 D102 p.607 The full account is in the chapter History.

The idea in one sentence. The letters do not describe a single justice: who judges, what is judged and the heaviest penalty change from one text to another. 1966D33-3Who judgesThe XANMOO (120 computers), under a single codeWhat is judgedcriminal responsibilityExtreme penalty“The death penalty does not exist”D33-3 p.491967D57-3Who judgesThe superior, on an expeditionWhat is judgedindisciplineExtreme penaltyphysical punishments “proscribed”, but possible “up to the loss of life”D57-3 p.2701967D68-1Who judgesThe OMMOI DOOXOO, humans; the machine does not judgeWhat is judgedconscious transgression onlyExtreme penaltyserving the communityD68-1 p.424D68-1 p.4271972D102Who judgesNot specifiedWhat is judgedtransgressionExtreme penaltypublic nudityD102 p.6071987D791Who judgesMachines: judge, jury, expertsWhat is judgedthe damage, not the intentionExtreme penalty“We neither chastise nor sanction”D791 p.855D791 p.856 Two contradictions stand out. On intent: in 1967, only a conscious act is punished; in 1987, consciousness is no longer assessed. On death: excluded in 1966, possible on an expedition in 1967. One can read in this an evolution of their society, an adaptation of the texts to their readers, or different authors; the chapter does not decide.

The comparison with thinkers and institutions of Earth is made by the author of the site; it sheds light on the ideas of the letters, and says nothing about their origin. On UmmoWhat is punishment for? To educate and repair, without vengeance Letter 1987 D791 p.855Immanuel Kant, 1797Punishing because the offence has been committed: retribution is a duty of justice.Cesare Beccaria, 1764, and Jeremy BenthamPunishing in order to prevent, at the fairest cost, and never beyond what is necessary.French Penal Code, art. 130-1The penalty must sanction and promote reform and reintegration.Analysis. The letters retain only one of the functions that our codes combine: reform. They set retribution aside entirely. This is consistent with their theology: the moral fault is settled elsewhere, by the BB after death, and society has only to correct. Without that later judgement, our societies leave to human justice the task of “repaying” evil.On UmmoPublic shame, brief and without mockery Letter 1972 D102 p.607Michel Foucault, 1975Discipline and Punish: the end of public torture and the shift to prison.John Braithwaite, 1989Crime, Shame and Reintegration: the shame that excludes (the pillory) is contrasted with “reintegrative” shame, expressed by the community and followed by forgiveness.Analysis. The 1972 scene is almost Braithwaite’s textbook example, seventeen years before him: the shame is real, but the public feels compassion and awaits the offender’s return. What distinguishes Ummo from the pillory is not the penalty but the attitude of the public. Our present-day equivalent would be exposure on social media, which is its exact opposite: public, mocking, endless and without return.On UmmoJudging the harm, not the intention Letter 1987 D791 p.856French Penal Code, art. 121-3“There is no crime or offence without the intent to commit it.”Spinoza, 1677Men believe themselves free because they are ignorant of the causes that determine them.Benjamin Libet, 1983; Robert Sapolsky, 2023Brain activity precedes the conscious decision; Sapolsky concludes from this, in Determined, that the notion of merit and fault must be abandoned.Analysis. The 1987 position is Sapolsky’s: if the act is determined, punishing the fault no longer makes sense, but protecting and correcting remain worthwhile. The letters add a nuance: freedom exists, but it is narrow and escapes human assessment. Our law makes the opposite bet: it judges intent because it assumes that it can be known.On UmmoMachines to judge Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49 Letter 1967 D68-1 p.427 Letter 1987 D791 p.855United States, the COMPAS toolIt assesses the risk of reoffending; the ProPublica investigation (2016) shows that it errs more often to the detriment of Black defendants.European Union, 2024The AI Regulation classes the administration of justice among “high-risk” uses: the machine may assist, the human must decide.Analysis. The 1967 letter adopts the position of our current European law. Those of 1966 and 1987 go further. Our experience shows the risk: a machine reproduces the biases of its data. The letters assume a machine without bias and a society without inequalities to reproduce, two conditions that we do not meet.On UmmoThe convict employed in experiments and labour Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49The US 13th Amendment, 1865It abolishes slavery except as a punishment: penal labour remains legal.Holmesburg Prison, 1950s-1970sInmates serve as subjects for dermatological and pharmaceutical experiments.Nuremberg Code, 1947The voluntary consent of the subject is “absolutely essential” to any experiment.Analysis. This is the point where the letters diverge most from our principles: the 1966 text regulates the practice (no pain, no mutilation, no death) but says nothing of consent. Our ethics, founded on Nuremberg, does the opposite: the subject’s will takes precedence over utility. The 1987 letters no longer mention it.On UmmoNeither prison nor vengeance: re-education Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49 Letter 1987 D791 p.855Norway, Halden Prison, 2010A life as normal as possible and a preparation for return.Howard Zehr, 1990Restorative justice: repairing the harm done to the victim and to the community rather than punishing.Analysis. The 1987 orientation (repair the damage, educate, do not take revenge) is that of restorative justice and of the Norwegian model, whose reoffending rates are among the lowest in Europe. The difference remains humiliation: our models set it aside, the letters use it as a lever.

Choices that we debate. Giving up retribution, judging the damage rather than the intent, entrusting the assessment to machines: each of these choices has a serious advocate on Earth (Braithwaite, Sapolsky, Zehr). A theological coherence. If the BB compensates the moral fault, human justice can limit itself to educating. Without this belief, our societies keep retribution, which partly explains why these reforms progress slowly among us. A clear limit. On consent, the 1966 letters fall short of our rules since Nuremberg.

The idea in one sentence. Besides the three doctrines, several points remain unexplained in the letters. Judging without judging intent: the 1987 letters say they do not assess awareness of the act, but take into account the person’s psychophysiological state, without specifying the boundary. Letter 1987 D791 p.855 D791 p.856“We neither chastise nor sanction”: the 1987 sentence coexists with the aversion shock and nakedness, which are sanctions in our vocabulary. Letter 1987 D791 p.855 Letter 1972 D102 p.607The “property of the People”: the status of the convict in 1966 is never mentioned again afterwards. Letter 1966 D33-3 p.49More women than men among those punished: the 1972 letter gives a gap of almost 23% without explaining it. Lafargue and the letters land on the same figure. Keynes was right about productivity, which has indeed multiplied, but wrong about free time: we chose to consume more rather than work less. Ummo nevertheless keeps a price mechanism for what is scarce: it is a planned economy for the abundant and a market economy for the scarce.On UmmoEach person’s account Letter 1966 D41-16 p.178Karl Marx, 1875Critique of the Gotha Programme: first “to each according to his work”, later “to each according to his needs”.China, 2014 planThe “social credit” system scores the behaviour of citizens and companies.Analysis. Ummo combines Marx’s two stages: needs are met for everyone, and work entitles one only to the scarce surplus. The comparison with social credit is useful by contrast: in the letters, the account measures what one contributes and does not penalise opinion. The only guarantee of this difference is the law, which leads back to the Justice chapter.On UmmoPower without privilege Letter 1967 D68-1 p.427 Letter 1967 D68-2 p.431Athens, 5th century BCSelection by lot and rapid rotation of offices.CincinnatusThe Roman dictator who returns to his plough once his task is done.Montesquieu, 1748The Spirit of the Laws: separating powers to prevent abuse.Analysis. The Council borrows from two traditions that we set against each other: the selection of the best (aristocracy in Plato’s sense) and the rotation that prevents entrenchment (Athenian democracy). According to the letters, it was born of a dictatorship: it is the same lesson we drew after the totalitarian regimes, when our constitutions limited terms of office.On UmmoNationalise the large, leave the small free, invest Late letter 1987 NR-23 p.1415 NR-23 p.1417France, 1945 and 1982Two waves of nationalisation of large companies and banks.Mondragon, since 1956A group of Basque cooperatives owned by their employees.Silvio Gesell, 1916; Keynes, 1936A currency that loses value if it is hoarded; the “paradox of thrift”, which slows activity.Analysis. The 1987 programme is almost word for word that of the European postwar mixed economy. Its originality lies in the morality underlying it: idle savings are “entropic”, hence immoral, while investment is “negentropic”. Keynes said the same thing as an economist; the letters make it a moral law.

A single decisive condition. The whole Ummite economy rests on an almost free material abundance. Free time, the absence of money and collective ownership follow from it. An ideal for Ummo, realism for us. When they advise the Earth, the letters propose neither abolishing money nor planning everything, but a mixed economy and an ethics of investment, close to our own post-war models. Thinkers already there. Plato for the elite without property, Lafargue and Keynes for free time, Marx for sharing according to needs: the letters assemble ideas that we know separately.

The letters do what Tetlock recommends: dated, quantified predictions. But their declared strategy of “counter-proofs” makes any test impossible in Popper’s sense: a correct prediction proves their knowledge, while a wrong one can pass for a deliberate decoy.

A view of their time. The letters’ diagnosis of submission, the media and consumption is that of the critical thinkers of the 1960s and 1970s (Fromm, Marcuse, Debord). Their model of the future overlaps with that of the Club of Rome, published the same year. One original feature: biology. Where our thinkers explain through economics or psychology, the letters explain through the brain, hormones and the collective soul. A mixed record of forecasts. Those that came true often extend visible tensions; the most precise and the most distant fail, with one notable exception.

The idea in one sentence. The letters themselves explain that they mix falsehood with truth, which makes any verification fragile; the chapter reports without settling the matter. The “counter-proofs”: as early as 1979, they say they spread false data mixed with true so that they would not be believed too readily; in 1984 and 1993, they congratulate themselves that this strategy has “borne fruit”. III · Different perspectives›Chapter 29 of 31Different perspectives · Chapter 29Jesus according to the letters In 1988, a long letter tells the life of Jesus and the birth of Christianity on the basis of documents that the authors say they unearthed in Israel, Egypt and Jordan. Their account departs from the Gospels on major points: Jesus would not have died on the cross. The chapter reports it, compares it with what historians and writers say, and points out the contradictions between the letters. This chapter reports claims that offend Christian faith. The authors themselves warn that they may “shock” and urge believers to remain faithful to their convictions Letter 1988 D792-3 p.906. an 8birth date given in 1988 (between 2 and 8 according to a call) D792-2 p.889 H17 p.13286condemned men crucified that day, Jesus included D792-2 p.8921 200 à 1 500witnesses of his disappearance D792-2 p.8941929claimed substitution of the Shroud of Turin D499 p.783

From the moment of their arrival, the expedition members are said to have taken an interest in “the strange figure of Jesus of Galilee”, because of his resemblance to their own divine man, UUMMOWOA Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889. Letter 1988 D499 p.781They write at first with caution, “so as not to hurt your religious feelings excessively”. Letter 1988 D792-1 p.860 The two lives side by side, according to the letters. For the letters, Jesus is an OEMMIIWOA: a being born of a rare mutation of the brain, directly linked with WOA, and not a god in the theologians’ sense Letter 1988 D792-1 p.881 Letter 1988 D505 p.786. He appears by chance, “orchestrated” by the collective soul, at very different moments depending on the planet: Jesus in a society still magical, UUMMOWOA in a scientific civilisation. Letter 1988 D792-1 p.881His genome would be different: he would be “the only representative of a different species” from Homo sapiens. Letter 1988 D505 p.786By telephone, in 1987: “In each OYAGAA a distinct Christ appears. A word, a piece of information was made flesh. This is a scientific truth.” Conversation 1987 H2 p.1272 Conversation 1987 H8 p.1303Such an envoy could be a woman. The letters recall the fate of Hypatia of Alexandria, a mathematician killed by a Christian mob in 415, to show what a woman claiming to be inhabited by God would have risked. Conversation 1987 H7 p.1299 Conversation 1987 H8 p.1303 The theory of the OEMMIIWOA is detailed in the chapter Spirituality.

The idea in one sentence. The letters say they rely on documents unknown to us, unearthed by three expedition members, but refuse to show them Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889 D792-2 p.894. O4OAROO 4, Y1YUU 1 and A6ADAA 66 are said to have travelled in Israel, Egypt and Jordan and, thanks to their detection techniques, dug up metal scrolls and inscriptions on stone and clay, now on Ummo. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889The passage by the historian Flavius Josephus on Christ would be entirely a Christian interpolation; Josephus “ignored or despised” Jesus. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889The “most reliable” text would be that of a disciple named Joram. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892They refuse to provide their proofs: doing so would oblige them to reveal who they are. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.894In 1988, two documents give, one year 8, the other year 3, for the birth; “the most probable interval is between 2 and 8”. Conversation 1988 H17 p.1327 H17 p.1328

h: 4 A life different from that of the Gospels
x: The idea in one sentence. Jesus would have been born in Galilee in a shepherds’ tent, would have been a disciple of John the Baptist before breaking with him, and would have gathered numerous, wealthy and even armed followers Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889 D792-2 p.890. Born not in Bethlehem but about twelve kilometres from Nazareth, in the eighth year of the era, to nomadic shepherd parents; he then has two brothers and a sister, followed by another brother. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889With shepherds from the surrounding area, he joins the Essenes who follow John the Baptist. When John preaches the assassination of Herod, Jesus publicly opposes it; John drives him away, and many of John’s followers follow the young disciple. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 D792-2 p.896Wealthy members of the Sanhedrin follow him in secret, attracted by his eloquence more than by his morality; one of them even plots against the High Priest. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.891His disciples had formed “an army”, organised by seven lieutenants, including Peter, James and John. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892 D792-2 p.893Pilate settles in Jerusalem with his legionaries, on the advice of Sejanus, Tiberius’s minister; Roman spies slip in among the disciples. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.891By telephone in 1988: the Jewish people were no more religious than others, Iran for example. Conversation 1988 H17 p.1329

The idea in one sentence. The letters’ account keeps the cross but changes almost everything else; it describes ill-treatment that the Gospels do not mention Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892. The episode in the Garden of Gethsemane would have no historical basis. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892The arrest takes place after the evening meal, at the house of Zhacar, a member of the Sanhedrin, where Jesus is surrounded by eighteen disciples, men and women. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892The High Priest hands him over to the Romans to avoid a split in the Sanhedrin. Pilate wants to humiliate him before the crowd: the letters describe a castration, a disguise as a woman and a crown made of a wicker cylinder studded with thorns. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892He is crucified at Golgotha with five other condemned men, not two. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892 The two accounts of the Passion. They diverge on the death and the tomb, then converge at the end: the sudden disappearance described by the letters and the “ascent to heaven” of the Gospels can be read as the same event, told in two languages.

The idea in one sentence. For the letters, Judas’s betrayal is a “slander” invented years later by the Jerusalem group Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893. Judas Iscariot was one of the most active lieutenants, a man of the people opposed to the wealthy disciples. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893On the evening of the arrest, he was camping with his supporters in the Garden of Gethsemane; warned, he launches a revolt in the streets of Jerusalem while Peter and others hide. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893He is captured, beaten to death, and his corpse is hung. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893The legend of the betrayal rests on a real fact: Rome and the High Priest did have paid agents among the disciples. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.891 D792-2 p.893

h: 7 He does not die on the cross
x: The idea in one sentence. “Jesus does not die”: recovered alive and cared for, he resumes his preaching, then disappears before the eyes of a crowd; it is this disappearance that would have become the Ascension Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890. Members of the Sanhedrin, secret disciples, bribe the Roman officer; at night, two legionaries let three disciples and two women through, who carry off the body, “almost dying”. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.892His death is made to be believed in order to avoid a new persecution; it is this version, taken up by the apologists, that becomes the resurrection. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890Recovered, he resumes his teaching; shortly afterwards, he suddenly disappears, “becomes transparent”, before twelve hundred to fifteen hundred people, shepherds, peasants and fishermen. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 D792-2 p.894 D792-2 p.895The first expedition members had at first believed that the disappearance had occurred on the cross; “a later analysis” of the documents is said to have corrected this idea. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893 D792-2 p.894By telephone in 1987, another version: the body of Jesus disappeared “when they die”, and the Ascension is “a myth”. Conversation 1987 H7 p.1299 Conversation 1987 H8 p.1303 The letters speak of a “distorted” account, but their disappearance and the Ascension of the Gospels basically describe the same scene: a man suddenly vanishing before his disciples’ eyes. For witnesses with no language other than that of their faith, saying that he “rises to heaven” was a poetic way, and probably the only possible one, of telling the inexplicable.

The idea in one sentence. In 1987 and in January 1988, the Shroud “wrapped the body of Jesus”; in November 1988, after the carbon-14 dating, the letters claim that the dated cloth is a fake substituted in 1929 Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 Letter 1988 D499 p.783. The imprint would come from medicinal plants, including aloe, placed on the wounds: this is the “vaporographic” thesis of Dr Paul Vignon (1902). The idea of a mysterious radiation is judged “absurd”. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 Letter 1988 D505 p.787The original cloth would have been kept by a witness of the disappearance, a peasant named Ismahi (or Semah), then by Stephen, before passing through Edessa and the Templars. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 Letter 1988 D505 p.787The still-liquid blood proved that Jesus was alive when he was wrapped: this is why, according to them, a small group within the Catholic hierarchy replaced it with a copy in 1929. Letter 1988 D499 p.783 Letter 1988 D505 p.788 D505 p.792They describe how the copy was made: a heated metal statue, electrical resistors, acid washes. Letter 1988 D505 p.790They call a meeting in Madrid on 20 November 1988 to “denounce” the fraud, and judge the matter more serious than many mass crimes for the evolution of humanity. Letter 1988 D490 p.775 D490 p.776 Letter 1988 D518 p.794 In orange, the dates of the letters; in pink, established facts. The explanation of the substitution appears only after the announcement of the carbon-14 result, on 13 October 1988.

The idea in one sentence. After the disappearance, the disciples split; the letters date each text of the New Testament and attribute several of them to other authors Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893 D792-2 p.897. The disciples split into four groups; the Jerusalem one, led by Peter, James and John, invents the number of twelve apostles to give itself authority. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893 D792-2 p.896Stephen, leader of the Hellenists, is killed by Zealots; Paul of Tarsus, a former Zealot, is initiated by a Hellenist named Thaïs, a witness of the disappearance. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.896A sect develops from the year 38 to 129-133, carried by the witnesses and their descendants. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.894The dates given: the Gospel of Mark before 52, Revelation in 79 by an exile named Naur, the Epistle of James between 78 and 81, Matthew in 82-84 at Antioch, John in 96 at Smyrna. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.897The Eucharist becomes a sacrament around 118; the institution of the Church arises between 170 and 243. The Gnostics represented a “more purified” Christianity, equally distorted but closer to science. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.897 D792-2 p.899 D792-2 p.900 The bands give the most common ranges among historians; the dots, the dates of the letters. For Mark and Revelation, the letters are markedly earlier.

The idea in one sentence. “The ecclesial phenomenon has done more harm than good to humanity”: the letters draw a sharp distinction between Jesus’s message and the institution that claims it Letter 1988 D792-2 p.898. They acknowledge the goodness of many Christians and the courage of the first martyrs, but judge that temporal power has corrupted the Church since Constantine. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.898They cite the witch hunts, the St Bartholomew’s Day massacre, the death of Giordano Bruno, and 20th-century crimes committed with the support of members of the clergy. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.898Those who wanted to reform the Church from within were isolated or eliminated: Francis of Assisi, John XXIII, Archbishop Romero; they claim that John Paul I was poisoned. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.899Already in 1980: “You have turned the sublime contributions of Jesus into an accumulation of superstitious ideas.” Letter 1980 D118 p.685In 1988, their plan of intervention nevertheless envisages a society founded on “moral bases inspired by the OEMMIIWOA Jesus of Galilee”. Letter 1988 D1378 p.920

The comparison with thinkers and institutions of Earth is made by the author of the site; it sheds light on the ideas of the letters, and says nothing about their origin. On UmmoA historical Jesus, distinct from the Jesus of the Gospels Letter 1988 D792-2 p.894Reimarus, published in 1778; David Strauss, 1835The first to separate the Jesus of history from the Christ of faith.Ernest Renan, 1863Life of Jesus: an admirable man, without miracles.Albert Schweitzer, 1906Each age fashions the Jesus who resembles it.Analysis. The letters themselves cite Renan, Loisy and Bultmann, and side with the “historical school” against the “mythological school” that denied Jesus’s existence. They claim to fill its gaps with documents that cannot be found. Schweitzer’s remark applies to them too: their Jesus is a biological and rational being, in the image of their own thinking.On UmmoThe passage of Flavius Josephus would be a forgery Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889John P. Meier, 1991; Géza VermesMost historians judge that the passage was altered by Christian copyists, but not invented from scratch.Shlomo Pines, 1971A more sober Arabic version, cited by Agapius in the 10th century, supports the idea of an authentic core.Analysis. The letters adopt the most radical position, that of a complete interpolation, which is now a minority view. The fact that a second passage of Josephus mentions “James, the brother of Jesus called Christ” is not discussed.On UmmoA birth in Galilee, around the year 2 to 8 Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889 Conversation 1988 H17 p.1328The historiansJesus would have been born before the death of Herod (4 BC), probably in Nazareth; Bethlehem belongs to theology.The Gospel of LukeIt places the birth at the census of Quirinius, in the year 6 of our era.Analysis. On the place, the letters agree with the majority of historians. On the date, they depart from them, but arrive at the one that Luke suggests (the census of the year 6), which historians judge incompatible with Matthew. They thus settle a known contradiction of the Gospels, without saying so.On UmmoJesus as a disciple of John the Baptist Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 D792-2 p.896John P. Meier, E. P. SandersThe baptism of Jesus by John is one of the best-established facts; many think he was first his disciple.Analysis. This is the point where the letters come closest to the historians. They add to it a violent break over a plan to murder Herod, of which no known source speaks.On UmmoJesus survived the cross Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 D792-2 p.892Karl Venturini, c. 1800; Heinrich Paulus, 1828The “swoon” theory: Jesus, believed dead, would have been revived.The Qur’an, surah 4, verse 157“They neither killed nor crucified him; but it was only a semblance” (Hamidullah’s French translation).Hugh Schonfield, 1965The Passover Plot: Jesus would have arranged his own survival.Analysis. The idea is not new: it runs through two centuries of biblical criticism and remains a living belief in Ahmadi Islam. Historians almost all reject it, since Roman crucifixion was designed to kill. The originality of the letters lies in what follows: a physical disappearance, before a crowd, explained by the physics of two universes. One is also reminded of Paul, who speaks of an appearance to “more than five hundred brethren at once”.On UmmoJudas rehabilitated Letter 1988 D792-2 p.893The Gospel of Judas, published in 2006A 2nd-century Gnostic text in which Judas is the disciple who understands Jesus best.Jorge Luis Borges, 1944“Three Versions of Judas”: the betrayal as the greatest sacrifice.Mikhail Bulgakov, The Master and MargaritaJudas is murdered there on Pilate’s orders.Analysis. The letters of 1988 rehabilitate Judas eighteen years before the publication of the Gospel of Judas, but differently: not as a confidant of Jesus, but as the leader of a popular revolt, killed by the authorities. Their version is more political than mystical, closer to Bulgakov than to the Gnostic text.On UmmoGospels written earlier, by others Letter 1988 D792-2 p.897The consensus of historiansMark around 70, Matthew around 80-90, John around 90-110, Revelation around 95; the real authors are unknown.Analysis. For Matthew and John, the dates of the letters fall within the historians’ ranges. For Mark (before 52) and Revelation (79), they are markedly earlier. The letters add names of authors (Naur, Daniel the Jew) that no source knows, and place the destruction of the Temple “until the year 49”, whereas it took place in 70.On UmmoThe Shroud of Turin Letter 1988 D499 p.783 Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890Paul Vignon, 1902The “vaporography” thesis that the letters take up.Nature, 16 February 1989Three laboratories date the cloth between 1260 and 1390.Pierre d’Arcis, 1389The Bishop of Troyes already denounces a painting.Analysis. The letters find an explanation that reconciles everything: a genuine shroud and a medieval result. But this explanation appears only after the announcement of the result, and it cannot be verified since the original would have disappeared. It is the same pattern as for their predictions: a claim that no fact can refute.

A Jesus of modern criticism. The letters’ account assembles theses known among us: Renan’s historical Jesus, the survival of the cross proposed by 19th-century rationalists, the rehabilitation of Judas, the distrust of the institution. It is consistent with their own doctrine: a biological envoy, a physical disappearance, a Church that betrays the message. Details without proof. The names (Zhacar, Joram, Thaïs, Naur) and the figures (eighteen disciples, five condemned men, 1,200 witnesses) rest on documents that they say they keep on Ummo. A literary account. By its force and its details, it belongs to the tradition of the “other Gospels” of Bulgakov, Kazantzakis (The Last Temptation, 1955) or Saramago (The Gospel According to Jesus Christ, 1991).

The idea in one sentence. The versions change from one letter and one call to another; the chapter reports them side by side. Death or survival: by telephone in 1987, the envoys “disappear when they die”; in the January 1988 letter, Jesus does not die on the cross and disappears later. Conversation 1987 H7 p.1299 Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890The Shroud: authentic in 1987 and in January 1988; in November 1988, after the dating, the object in Turin becomes a copy from 1929. Conversation 1987 H7 p.1299 Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 Letter 1988 D499 p.783Its keeper: a peasant named Ismahi in one letter, Semah or Semahel in another. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.890 Letter 1988 D505 p.787The date of birth: year 8 in the letter; between year 2 and year 8, with a document giving year 3, by telephone. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.889 Conversation 1988 H17 p.1328The Temple: destroyed at the end of a revolt “until the year 49” according to the letter, in 70 according to history. Letter 1988 D792-2 p.896The proofs: the unearthed documents, the 1929 copy and the assassination of John Paul I are supported by no accessible source. The letters describe these investigations without supplying the images or recordings. ch: Parapsychology: the letters unmask the frauds
x: The idea in one sentence. For the letters, parapsychology is not a science but a waiting room: a phenomenon stays there as long as its laws are unknown, then it passes to psychology or disappears Letter 1967 D62-2 p.359. Among us the word denotes a mixture: telepathy, clairvoyance, precognition, ectoplasm, hypnosis, telekinesis, haunted houses, dowsing, the prodigies of the Brahmins. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.359Hypnosis is the example: long doubted, it was accepted in the early twentieth century and left the category. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.359The letters cite the researchers who tried to separate truth from falsehood: Charles Richet, Karl von Reichenbach, William Crookes. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.359Telepathy is “very familiar” to them; they smile at the explanations of the psychiatrists of Duke University. Ectoplasm and spirit photography, on the other hand, are “totally unknown” on Ummo and “fill them with stupefaction”. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.362This is what launches the investigation: a group led by Y6YOA 6, son of U5UNOO 532, leaves for New Delhi and Boston. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.362 Telepathy as the letters describe it is dealt with in the Telepathy chapter.

ch: Parapsychology: the letters unmask the frauds
x: The idea in one sentence. Neither believing nor denying on principle: the letters call for an “active doubt” that methodically rules out all ordinary causes before studying what remains Letter 1967 D62-2 p.360 D62-2 p.361. Faced with a UFO witness, the first reaction should be “prudent scepticism”. But an “immobilist” incredulity, which denies without analysing, is judged just as faulty. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.360Four hypotheses must be ruled out: lying, delusion, illusion or hallucination, and confusion with an aeroplane, a weather balloon, a meteor, a large bird or a rare ball lightning. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.360A single proof is not enough: collective testimonies, analysed photo negatives and measured traces, all together. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.360They do not reproach scientists for their mistrust: without these “mental barriers”, science would have been drowned by impostors and the deluded. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.361But one must not give up: without Rhine’s statistical methods, telepathy would have been filed away with necromancy. Letter 1967 D62-2 p.361 D62-2 p.362The conclusion of the series says it again: shun “excessive credulity” as much as “fanatical scepticism”; failing an investigation, keep a “prudent attitude of listening”. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.393 The witness sieve, after the 1967 letter. Each tier rules out an ordinary explanation; only what passes all four deserves study, and then with all the evidence at once.

ch: Parapsychology: the letters unmask the frauds
x: The idea in one sentence. The most famous experiment of metapsychics, the casting of “spirit” hands in paraffin wax, is said to have been unmasked by two investigators equipped with infrared cameras Letter 1967 D62-3 p.364 D62-3 p.365 D62-3 p.366. They discover ectoplasm in the Revue métapsychique, in Paris, then in the work of Gustave Geley with the Polish medium Franek Kluski, and in Richet’s Traité de métapsychique. Letter 1967 D62-3 p.363 D62-3 p.364The protocol they summarise: closed room, medium held by the sleeves in the dark, a tub of secretly marked paraffin. In the light, two one-piece hand moulds, with foreign prints. Letter 1967 D62-3 p.364 D62-3 p.365Their fundamental objection: imagining a soul without dimension “equipped with arms and hands” ready to dip into the wax strikes them as “childish”. Letter 1967 D62-3 p.365In 1959, in Los Angeles, G6GIIA 64 and A7AARAA 7 present themselves as Norwegian spiritist doctors at a séance of “Mrs Mc Lean”, with hidden infrared and ultraviolet cameras. Letter 1967 D62-3 p.365 D62-3 p.366The images show the medium making the two men hold each other, taking three elastic gloves out of her underwear, inflating them, dipping them several times in the paraffin, then deflating them. The prints came from a plaster cast of a real hand. Letter 1967 D62-3 p.366Thirty-two other séances in Mexico, the United States and England: gauze and muslin on steel wire, fluorescent polyurethane foam. No real materialisation. Letter 1967 D62-3 p.366They do not conclude from this that it does not exist: “show us a single case of ectoplasmy and we will accept it”. Letter 1967 D62-3 p.366 The glove trick, as the letter describes it. The wax shell, deprived of the hand that formed it, passes for the mould of a hand that was materialised and then dissolved.

ch: Parapsychology: the letters unmask the frauds
h: 4 The Indian rope trick: the investigation
x: The idea in one sentence. In 1957, the investigators say they finally saw what no one had been able to film: a rope that rises by itself and up which a child climbs Letter 1967 D62-4 p.369 D62-4 p.370 D62-4 p.371. They knew the accounts: Johann Weyer in the sixteenth century, the magician Howard Thurston who went to India in vain in 1920, an article by the journalist Keel in the magazine Argosy. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.369A first attempt fails: travelling with false Irish passports, they have to flee the police, after destroying their equipment. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.369Disguised as agents of a Pakistani tea firm, they wait four days for an old saddu, paid in pounds sterling. On 7 April 1957, some twenty villagers accompany them; an observation sphere follows them at an altitude of 800 m. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.370The old man stares at a coil of rope. The knot emerges, the rope rises, undulating: seven metres in 4.37 minutes. A child climbs it and comes back down; the rope falls back in loops. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.371They admit to having remained “perplexed”: as specialists in sleight of hand, they had expected to find the trick with the naked eye. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.371

ch: Parapsychology: the letters unmask the frauds
x: The idea in one sentence. That very evening, a probe buried in the ground reveals the trick: the “rope” is an iron bar sheathed in fibres, pushed up from below by an accomplice Letter 1967 D62-4 p.373 D62-4 p.374 D62-4 p.375. The investigators pretend to leave, return by night and launch a XOIMMA UGII, an ellipsoid that sinks into the rock, vaporising it beneath a layer of plasma. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.373At fifty or a hundred metres underground, it moves about and detects cavities, tubes and objects of more than five centimetres. On the surface, only a pin is found. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.373 D62-4 p.374The explanation: from an underground gallery, an accomplice hooks the knot passed through a tube, pulls the rope and at the same time hoists an iron bar covered with fibres of the same colour. A wedge locks it; the child can climb. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.375The coil hides the operation from the spectators, who see the rope “unrolling” and rising. Letter 1967 D62-4 p.375Their comment: “If all the genius wasted by Terrestrials to deceive their brothers were used to organise society better…” Letter 1967 D62-4 p.375 The set-up described by the letter, in section. Above ground, the audience sees a rope rise; below, an accomplice hoists a rigid bar that carries its sheath. The letters’ probes and observation spheres are presented in the Technologies chapter.

x: The idea in one sentence. ch: Parapsychology: the letters unmask the frauds
x: The idea in one sentence. Walking on embers is “not at all a fraud”, but not a parapsychological phenomenon either: it is physics Letter 1967 D62-7 p.390. Heat makes the feet sweat profusely. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.390In fine droplets of 0.07 mm, water cannot carry heat by convection; it becomes as insulating as a plastic. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.390They also invoke the experiment of drops bouncing on a plate at 300 °C without evaporating, protected by a layer of vapour. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.390They dismiss in passing an argument heard among believers: one cannot deny a prodigy merely because one did not witness it. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.389 D62-7 p.390

ch: Parapsychology: the letters unmask the frauds
x: The idea in one sentence. The letters reject neither healers nor folk remedies outright: they admit real but rare cases, and call for figures as proof Letter 1967 D62-7 p.391 D62-7 p.392. A healer who made a kidney tumour disappear by laying on hands cannot be denied without study; they say they have recognised “in the odd isolated case” such a “cryptotherapeutics”. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.391Most often, they find fraud, or a suggestion that makes the pain recede while the tumour remains. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.391Their argument in figures: even if all the post-war polio healers had been honest, compare the number of patients then with that of 1967, after the vaccines. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.391A share of popular beliefs nonetheless has a real basis: the mouldy bread of Greek fishermen before Fleming’s penicillin, the cod-liver oil of the Norwegian fjords. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.392They say they have studied KHUROYAKI, a Japanese rural medicine of sealed, heated pottery. Letter 1967 D62-7 p.392By telephone in 1987: magnetic passes give results that are “temporary but not definitive”. Conversation 1987 H7 p.1299 Ummo’s medicine is described in the Health and Medicine chapter.
